chapter_theme: The closing summary (கட்டுரை) of the Puhar book: a single long sentence lists what the first ten kaathais set out about the Chola line and its land (righteousness, valour, the old city, its festivals, the divine Kaveri, the unfailing sky) and about its arts of stage, dance, vari songs and the lute, all seen as one; a venba then wishes Puhar, built by fame for the sea-moated earth, to live like the morning sun and the evening moon.

silappathikaram:pukar_kandam_katturai:1-.reading: The narrator sums up the Puhar book as one that keeps in single view the righteousness, valour and strength of those born in the Chola line among the three crowned kings, the excellence of their ancient city, its festivals and the visits of the gods, the people and abundant food of their land, the evil-removing divine Kaveri, the unfailing sky pouring new floods, and the arts of stage, dance, rhythm, vari songs, the lute and its modes, and declares the book complete.
silappathikaram:pukar_kandam_katturai:1-.nuance: The same formula, nearly word for word, closes the Madurai and Vanchi books with the Pandya and Chera lines put in place of the Chola, so the praise of aram, maram and an unfailing sky belongs to the frame given every crowned line, not to a judgment on this one. What differs is the close: the Madurai summary looks at its book as one with the Pandya Nedunjeliyan who died on his throne with his queen, the Vanchi summary with Senguttuvan, while this one names no king and gives most of its lines to music and dance (lines 10 to 16, the arts of Madhavi's kaathais). The music terms of lines 13 to 16 (சகோடம், இடநிலைப் பாலை, தாரத்து ஆக்கம், ஊரகத் தேர்) are technical and are left unglossed here; the reading does not turn on them.

claims.claim: the divine Kaveri removes evil from the land it waters

silappathikaram:pukar_kandam_katturai:21.reading: A closing venba wishes that Puhar, which fame has made for the earth whose moat is the sea, may live on like the sun that buds and blooms in the morning and the moon of the evening.
silappathikaram:pukar_kandam_katturai:21.nuance: The wish for the city's lasting life is a blessing, not a claim that it will last; the poem calls the sea the earth's moat (வேலை அகழால் அமைந்த அவனி), the sea that the Manimekalai later makes the city's end. The kandam opened (silappathikaram:1:1-12) by praising the moon and the sun for being like the Chola; here they are the measure for the city, and no king is named.

links.note: Both praise the Chola land of Puhar through its water; the Pattinappalai grants that the sky may fail and makes the Kaveri the river that never fails, while the epic's summary sets the divine Kaveri beside a sky that itself never fails (பொய்யா வானம்).
links.teaches: The Sangam poem rests Puhar's plenty on the river precisely because the sky can fail, and the epic's summary removes that concession, making the sky unfailing too in a line it reuses unchanged for the Pandya land, so the pair shows a Puhar-specific boast about the Kaveri turning into a stock praise that any crowned line receives.

gains.a: the summary's unfailing sky gains a point of contrast: in the older praise of the same city it was the river, not the sky, that could be trusted
gains.b: the Pattinappalai's claim about the Kaveri gains a later form in which the river's distinction has been levelled into a formula shared by the three kingdoms

links.note: The two summaries share their opening lines word for word (aram, maram, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, food, the unfailing sky), with the Vaigai for the Kaveri; the Madurai summary ends by viewing its book as one with the Pandya Nedunjeliyan who died on his throne with his chaste queen, the Puhar summary names no king.
links.teaches: Because the praise of righteousness and unfailing rain is a fixed frame granted alike to the Chola line and to the Pandya whose verdict burned his city, the epic's judgment of a kingdom lies not in that praise but in what each summary sets at its centre: for Madurai a king who died of his own wrong, for Puhar no king at all but its arts.

links.note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules with the sceptre as it should be; the summary lists the Chola line's righteousness beside the unfailing sky and abundant food, and the Madurai summary gives the same lines to the Pandya line.
links.teaches: Set beside the couplet, the summaries' line of unfailing rain reads as the Kural's sign of just rule, yet the epic grants it equally to the line whose king it shows killing an innocent man, so the pair shows the epic keeping the sign as ceremony while placing the real test of the sceptre in a single verdict.

gains.a: the formula's rain line gains the political meaning the couplet gives it, as a claim that the realm is justly ruled
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its sign of good rule is ascribed to a kingdom whose sceptre the story will show bent, which shows that the sign alone cannot vouch for the king

links.note: The venba wishes Puhar, made by fame for the earth whose moat is the sea, to live like the sun and the moon; the Manimekalai tells that when the king, searching for his lost son, left off the Indra festival, Manimekala Deivam bade the sea take the city.
links.teaches: The sea the venba names only as the earth's protecting moat is the agent that takes the city in the sequel, and the festival the summary counts among Puhar's glories is the rite whose neglect brings it, so the blessing of lasting life holds the terms of its own reversal.

links.note: The Puhar book opens hailing the moon, the sun and Puhar for resembling the Chola's umbrella, wheel and line, and closes wishing Puhar to live like the morning sun and the evening moon.
links.teaches: The book is framed by the same sun, moon and city, but at the opening the heavenly bodies are praised as likenesses of the king, and at the close they are the measure of the city's own life with the king gone from the comparison, matching a summary that names the Chola line but no Chola.

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: the unit names the lute (யாழ் line 13) and the mode (பண் line 15); இசை in line 11 means fame; id as used in the Valayapathi and Silappathikaram 7 marks

source_issues: Line 4 was repaired from a TSCII leftover (ு + ட read as ூ), as show flags.
The chapter header counts 24 lines but the edition's last printed number is 20: the closing venba is numbered 21 to 24 by the tool, not by the edition.

Line 19 (ஒரு பரிசா நோக்கிக் கிடந்த) has no named king with ஓடு before it, unlike the Madurai summary (பாண்டியன் நெடுஞ்செழியனோடு) and the Vanchi summary (செங்குட்டுவனோடு) built on the same frame; the text does not show whether the Puhar summary names no king by design or a line is lost.
Line 20 (புகார்க் காண்டம் முற்றிற்று) is a colophon that also completes the sentence of lines 1 to 19 (கிடந்த governs காண்டம்), so it is marked as part of the unit.
